claims.text: A silicide coating can be applied by pack cementation.
Pack cementation will create a uniform, silicon-rich layer on a boride-based component.
Applying a thin silicide coating will improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of boride-based components.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating immersion temperatures are approximately 700–800 °C.
The coating will form a dense, adherent silicide layer.
The dense, adherent silicide layer will act as a diffusion barrier.
The silicide coating will limit aluminum diffusion into the boride substrate.
Limiting aluminum diffusion into the boride substrate will reduce molten-aluminum attack.
Oxidation products or reaction with aluminum may locally seal microcracks in the silicide coating.
Local sealing of microcracks will maintain the coating's barrier function during thermal cycling.
Silicide-coated components may exhibit approximately a tenfold reduction in corrosion rate relative to uncoated boride-based components.
Reducing the corrosion rate will extend component service life during aluminum-plating operations.
As-fabricated, uncoated boride-based components suffer rapid corrosion in contact with molten aluminum.
The silicide coating should remain protective under standard hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
Excessively high temperatures, prolonged exposure, or large or interconnected cracks may diminish coating effectiveness.
Compatibility problems may occur between the silicide coating and the boride substrate.
Coated and uncoated batches should be compared by molten-aluminum immersion at 700–800 °C using weight loss, aluminum-penetration depth, and coating-integrity measurements.
The hypothesis is falsified if the coating provides less than a twofold improvement in corrosion rate or degrades significantly under standard operating conditions.
